explanations.explanation: The text says she left him "…to return to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah." So she went back to where she came from. I think that tells you how things stood between the two of them at that point. Her dad's house is where this whole next stretch of the story happens.

I get why a brother might come to mind, friend, but no brother shows up anywhere in this passage. The text says she went back to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah. Her dad is the one who gladly welcomes the Levite when he arrives. So keep your eye on the father.

Micah is a man from the hill country of Ephraim earlier in Judges (Judges 17:1), but he isn't in this story at all. The text says she went back to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah. That's the only house she heads for here. Different chapter, different guy.

explanations.answer: Speak kindly to her and bring her back
explanations.explanation: The text says her husband went after her "…to speak kindly to her and bring her back…" That's a long trip with a servant and a pair of donkeys, so he means business. That's what the passage tells us about why he went.

Money never comes up in this trip, baker. The text says he went after her "…to speak kindly to her and bring her back…" No bill, no demands, nothing like that. It's all about getting her to come home.

explanations.answer: Bring her before the town elders
explanations.explanation: That would be a whole courtroom scene, and the text doesn't have one. It says he went after her "…to speak kindly to her and bring her back…" There are no elders in this part of the story. Just a husband, a servant, two donkeys and a long road.

It's the other way around, friend. The text says that when her father saw the Levite, "…he gladly welcomed him." There's no frown and no cold shoulder here. The girl brings him in, and her dad is happy to see him.

Right, because the text says her father "…gladly welcomed him." The girl brings the Levite into the house, and her dad is glad he's there. That's the whole mood of the scene. Hold on to it, because the story won't stay this warm.

explanations.answer: Have a bite of bread before you go
explanations.explanation: That's it. The father says, "Refresh your heart with a morsel of bread, and then you can go." Just a little bread, and then he can leave. Sounds like me with a batch. 'One more cookie' is how every long goodbye starts.

explanations.answer: The roads are too dangerous today
explanations.explanation: The father never says anything about the roads. What he says is, "Refresh your heart with a morsel of bread, and then you can go." It's a friendly offer of food at the door. He doesn't give a warning.

explanations.answer: My daughter is not ready to leave
explanations.explanation: The father doesn't say that, baker. The text has him say, "Refresh your heart with a morsel of bread, and then you can go." It's about a little bread, and it doesn't mention his daughter. I'd stick to what he actually says.

He does get up early, but that's as far as it goes. The father says, "Please refresh your heart." and the text says they "…waited until late afternoon and the two of them ate." Early morning plans turned into a late afternoon meal. That's a long way from being on the road by morning.

That's right. The Levite gets up early to depart, but the father says, "Please refresh your heart." So they wait until late afternoon and eat. Getting up early to leave and still being at the table in late afternoon are two very different things.

The text says "…the man was unwilling to spend the night. He got up and departed…" He leaves with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine, and the servant is still with them. After all those requests from his father-in-law, he finally doesn't stay.

explanations.answer: Asks to stay a whole week
explanations.explanation: A week is a long stretch, friend, and the text doesn't have him ask for it. The text says "…the man was unwilling to spend the night." He doesn't ask for a week, because he won't take even one more night. He gets up and goes.

The text doesn't send anybody off by himself. It says the man "…got up and departed…" and reached the area near Jebus with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine. The servant is still with him a few verses later (Judges 19:11). Everybody leaves together.

explanations.answer: Stop and spend the night in Jebus
explanations.explanation: The servant says, "Please, let us stop at this Jebusite city and spend the night here." The day is almost gone, so it sounds like a plain, practical idea to me. The text says Jebus is Jerusalem (Judges 19:10). The servant is the one asking here, and the Levite answers him next.

explanations.answer: Turn back to the house in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Nobody says to turn back, baker. The servant says, "Please, let us stop at this Jebusite city and spend the night here." The day is almost gone and he wants to stop in the city they're near. Bethlehem is behind them and doesn't come up.

explanations.answer: Keep walking all through the night
explanations.explanation: That's not what the servant says. He says, "Please, let us stop at this Jebusite city and spend the night here." It's the opposite of walking all night. He wants them to stop for the night.

Yes. The Levite says, "We will not turn aside to the city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites." He gives his reason right there: no Israelites live in that city. So he tells his servant they'll go on to Gibeah instead.

The word idols isn't in what he says. The Levite says, "We will not turn aside to the city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites." The only reason he gives is that no Israelites live there. I'd stick to his exact words.

Soldiers don't come up here, friend. What the Levite says is, "We will not turn aside to the city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites." He says nothing about an army. His whole reason is that it's a city with no Israelites.

True, and it's a hard moment. The sun set as they neared Gibeah, and the Levite went in and sat down in the city square, "…but no one would take them into his home for the night." I think it's a lonely feeling to sit there with nobody opening a door.
I wish that were true, friend. The text says the Levite sat down in the city square, "…but no one would take them into his home for the night." Nobody opens a door. It's a rough way to end the day.

explanations.answer: Where he is going and where he came from
explanations.explanation: That's what he asks: "Where are you going, and where have you come from?" The old man has come in from his work in the field and spots the traveler sitting in the square. It's a simple question, and the Levite answers all of it. He starts a conversation with the traveler.

explanations.answer: Whether he can pay for a room tonight
explanations.explanation: The old man doesn't ask about money, baker. The text says he asked, "Where are you going, and where have you come from?" There's no price talk anywhere in this scene. His question is only about where the man is going and where he came from.

explanations.answer: Why he brought his donkeys into town
explanations.explanation: The donkeys don't get a question, though the old man does take care of them later (Judges 19:21). What he asks is, "Where are you going, and where have you come from?" His first words are about the man himself.

He says it himself: "I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the LORD…" He's heading home to Ephraim, and he names that as where he's going too. The text doesn't say more about his plan, so I'll leave it there.

Shechem isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage, friend. The Levite says he's traveling to the hill country of Ephraim, and "…now I am going to the house of the LORD…" He names Bethlehem, Ephraim and the house of the LORD, but never Shechem.
Bethel doesn't come up here, baker. The Levite says he's headed to Ephraim, where he's from, and "…now I am going to the house of the LORD…" He doesn't name Bethel at all.

The old man says, "Peace to you. Let me supply everything you need. Only do not spend the night in the square." That's a big, open-handed offer. I think after all those closed doors, it must have sounded like a whole new world. Notice the Levite said he lacked nothing, and the old man still offers to supply what he needs.

explanations.answer: To sell him food for the road
explanations.explanation: There's no sale in this scene. The old man says, "Let me supply everything you need." He's offering to take care of them, and he doesn't mention a price. The text shows him opening his home.

explanations.answer: To guide him on to Ramah
explanations.explanation: Ramah did come up earlier, when the Levite said they'd try to reach Gibeah or Ramah (Judges 19:13). But the old man doesn't offer to guide anybody there. He says, "Let me supply everything you need." He wants them to stay with him.

explanations.answer: This man is a guest in my house
explanations.explanation: That's his reason: "After all, this man is a guest in my house." He also calls it a wicked thing and an outrage. I think this is a heavy scene, so I'll just say plainly that the old man tells them to stop.

explanations.answer: This man is a priest of the LORD
explanations.explanation: The old man doesn't say that. The text has him say, "After all, this man is a guest in my house." Being a guest is the only reason he gives here. He also tells them, "Do not commit this outrage."

explanations.answer: This man has done nothing wrong
explanations.explanation: That's not what the old man says. He says, "After all, this man is a guest in my house." That's the reason he gives, and he tells them, "Do not commit this outrage." I'd stay with the words the text gives us.
They don't. The text says, "…the men would not listen to him." This is a very dark moment in the story, and I won't make light of it. What happens next is in that same verse (Judges 19:25).
That's right. The text says, "…the men would not listen to him." It's a heavy part of the story, friend. I think it's okay to feel how heavy it is.

She does. The text says that early that morning "…the woman went back to the house where her master was staying, collapsed at the doorway, and lay there until it was light." At dawn the men let her go, and that's where she goes. I think this is one of the hardest verses in the whole book.

She does go back, friend. The text says "…the woman went back to the house where her master was staying, collapsed at the doorway, and lay there until it was light." It's a painful picture. I think we should let it be as heavy as it is.

explanations.answer: Get up and let us go
explanations.explanation: The text has him say, "Get up. Let us go." Then it says, "But there was no response." That's all the passage gives us for his words to her. It stays heavy, and I think it's fair to say so.

explanations.answer: Forgive me for what I did
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have the Levite say that. His words to her are, "Get up. Let us go." Then it says, "But there was no response." Those are the only words we're given.

explanations.answer: Wait here while I find help
explanations.explanation: He doesn't say that, baker. The text has him say, "Get up. Let us go." And then, "But there was no response." That's what we're told, and it's a hard moment to read.

That's right. The text says he cut her into twelve pieces "…and sent her throughout the territory of Israel." It's a grim scene, and I'll keep it simple. What the people say when they see it comes in the next verse.

Jebus came up earlier, when the servant wanted to stop there (Judges 19:11), and the Levite said no. It isn't where he sends the pieces. The text says he sent her "…throughout the territory of Israel." That's a much wider reach.

Her father is in Bethlehem, but the text doesn't say he sent anything only there. It says the Levite sent her "…throughout the territory of Israel." That's all of Israel, and not one house. It's a heavy verse, friend.

Yes. Everyone who saw it said, "Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day." They're pointing back to the day the Israelites came out of Egypt. So the people were saying nothing like this had been seen or done in all that time.

Babylon isn't what the people say, baker. They say, "Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day." Egypt is the place they name. So Egypt is the answer.

Haran is a place in Abraham's story (Genesis 11:31), but it isn't what the people say here. They say, "Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day." So Egypt is the answer. They're looking back to the day the Israelites came out of Egypt.
It's the opposite, friend. The people say, "Think it over, take counsel, and speak up!" That's a call to talk about it, not to stay quiet. The story isn't done yet, and I think we can feel that.
Right. They say, "Think it over, take counsel, and speak up!" That means think, talk it over and say something. It's a serious moment, and I'd say the people knew it. The story isn't over, though.
